mainTopic: Neighbors' rights when building: a sunken two-story house, a wall that blocks a neighbor's windows, and brothers who split an estate and argue over a hall's light.
overview: This amud has three stories about neighbors and building. In the first, the lower floor of a house has sunk. רב חמא rules that the upstairs owner can stop the downstairs owner from rebuilding, unless the beams have sunk below ten טפחים or the two owners agreed ahead of time to rebuild. If they agreed, רבה says they rebuild once the space is no longer livable the normal way. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע measures that as room to carry in a bundle of מחוזא reeds and turn around. In the second story, a man builds a wall that darkens his neighbor's windows. The neighbor turns down every offer the builder makes, and רב חמא rules that he can stop the wall, even if the room is used only for storage. In the third story, two brothers split an estate, and the one who got the garden builds a wall in front of his brother's hall. Here רב חמא lets him build. רבינא and רב אשי then debate why, and the גמרא ends by rejecting a proof from sales: brothers split an estate expecting to live as their fathers did. The amud closes as a new reply to רב חמא begins, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The two neighbors argue over rebuilding the sunken house
steps.stepSummary: The downstairs owner offers to rebuild and even to rent the upstairs owner a temporary home. The upstairs owner refuses and tells him to crawl in and out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The downstairs owner said: I will tear it down and rebuild it. The upstairs owner said: I have nowhere to live in the meantime. The downstairs owner said: I will rent you a place. The upstairs owner said: I don't want the bother. The downstairs owner said: But I can't live like this! The upstairs owner answered: Crawl in on your belly and crawl out on your belly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells the back-and-forth between the two neighbors. This sets up the legal question of who is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The downstairs owner answers every objection, even offering to pay for temporary housing. The upstairs owner still refuses only because moving is a bother. This makes the case sharp: is someone allowed to block a repair just because he doesn't want the hassle?

keyTerms.meaning: I don't want to go to the trouble

phrases.english: He said to him: "I will tear it down and rebuild it."
phrases.notes: The downstairs owner is speaking. His floor has sunk into the ground.

phrases.english: He said: "I have no place to live in."
phrases.notes: Now the upstairs owner answers. He means while the house is being rebuilt.

phrases.english: He said to him: "I will rent a place for you."
He said to him: "I don't want the bother."
"But I can't live here!"
phrases.notes: This is the downstairs owner again. His ceiling is now too low to live under.

phrases.english: "Crawl on your belly and go in,"
and crawl on your belly and go out."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֶיסְתְּרֵיהּ אֲנָא וְאֶבְנְיֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the sunken house from before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet; this sets out the facts of the dispute.

steps.title: רב חמא: the upstairs owner may legally block the rebuilding
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא rules that the upstairs owner is within his rights to stop the rebuilding.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חמא said: By law, he can block it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חמא gives the ruling on the story. The upstairs owner is legally allowed to prevent the downstairs owner from tearing the house down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the upstairs owner's reason seems weak, he has a right to his living space as it is. He cannot be forced out against his will, even with a rental offered.

phrases.english: Rav Chama said:
By law he can block it.
phrases.notes: "He" is the upstairs owner who refused.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָמָא: בְּדִינָא קָא מְעַכֵּב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the dispute told in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The upstairs owner can legally block the rebuilding.

steps.title: First limit: only if the beams have not sunk below ten טפחים
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא's ruling applies only while the beams are still above ten טפחים. Below that, the space belongs to the downstairs owner alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only when the beams have not dropped below ten טפחים. But if they have dropped below ten, the downstairs owner can say: Below ten is my space, and it is not bound to serve you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רב חמא's ruling by adding a first exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The upstairs owner's rights reach down only to ten טפחים. Once the ceiling beams sink lower than that, they are sitting in the downstairs owner's own space. Then the downstairs owner may rebuild.

phrases.english: And this applies only
when the beams have not reached below ten,
phrases.notes: These are the beams that hold up the upper floor. Ten means ten טפחים from the ground.

phrases.english: but if the beams have reached below ten,
he can say to him:
"Below ten is my domain,"
and it is not bound to you."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּלָא מָטוּ כְּשׁוּרֵי לְמַטָּה מֵעֲשָׂרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ruling of step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the beams sink below ten טפחים, the downstairs owner may rebuild.

steps.title: Second limit: unless they agreed ahead of time to rebuild
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא's ruling also applies only when the two owners made no agreement. If they agreed to rebuild, they tear it down and rebuild.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this applies only when they did not make a condition with each other. But if they did make a condition with each other, they tear it down and rebuild.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second exception to רב חמא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier agreement between the owners overrides the upstairs owner's right to refuse. If they agreed that a sunken house would be rebuilt, he must go along with it.

keyTerms.meaning: they made a condition; they stipulated

phrases.aramaic: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּלָא אַתְנוֹ גַּבֵּי הֲדָדֵי,
phrases.english: And this applies only when they did not make a condition with each other,
but if they did make a condition with each other,
they tear it down and rebuild.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּלָא אַתְנוֹ גַּבֵּי הֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit to the ruling of step 2, alongside step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An agreement to rebuild obligates both owners to tear down and rebuild.

steps.title: How far must the ceiling sink before the agreement applies?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks at what point the agreement to rebuild comes into effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when they did make a condition with each other: how far must it sink?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question about the agreement from step 4. This sets up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying "we will rebuild if it sinks" is vague. The גמרא wants to know how much sinking is enough to trigger the agreement.

keyTerms.meaning: up to how much? how far?

phrases.english: And when they made a condition with each other,
how far must it sink?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי אַתְנוֹ בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי עַד כַּמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details of the agreement in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The measurement at which an agreement to rebuild comes into effect.

steps.title: An answer quoted in רב נחמן's name: height is half the length plus half the width
steps.stepSummary: The scholars, quoting רב נחמן, compare this to the משנה about a house built for someone else. Its height should be half its length plus half its width.
steps.simpleTranslation: The scholars said before רבה, in the name of מר זוטרא son of רב נחמן, who said it in the name of רב נחמן: It is like what we learned in the משנה: its height is half its length plus half its width.
steps.whatsHappening: An answer to step 5 is offered, borrowing a measurement from a different משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the lower floor must keep the standard height of a house. If it drops below that height, the agreement to rebuild applies. This would be a fairly demanding standard.

phrases.english: The scholars said before Rabba

phrases.aramaic: מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּמָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: in the name of Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman,
who said in the name of Rav Nachman:
Like what we learned:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה later in this מסכת (98b) about someone who builds a house for another person.

phrases.english: Its height is like half its length plus half its width.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ רַבָּנַן קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The house must keep a standard house's height: half its length plus half its width.

steps.title: רבה rejects that quote: רב נחמן said 'as people normally live'
steps.stepSummary: רבה scolds the scholars for pinning a foolish opinion on רב נחמן. He says רב נחמן's real view is that the space must be livable in the normal way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to them: Didn't I tell you not to hang empty pitchers on רב נחמן? This is what רב נחמן actually said: as people normally live.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה rejects the answer from step 6. He says it was quoted wrongly, and he gives רב נחמן's true words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה holds that רב נחמן never required the full standard house height. The real rule is a lower bar: rebuilding is required only once the space is too low to live in normally.

phrases.english: Rabba said to them:
Didn't I tell you:

phrases.aramaic: לָא תִּיתְלוֹ בֵּיהּ בּוּקֵי סְרִיקֵי בְּרַב נַחְמָן?!
phrases.english: Do not hang empty pitchers on Rav Nachman?!
phrases.notes: In other words, don't put silly opinions in רב נחמן's mouth.

phrases.english: This is what Rav Nachman said:
As people normally live.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָאו אָמֵינָא לְכוּ: לָא תִּיתְלוֹ בֵּיהּ בּוּקֵי סְרִיקֵי בְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects how step 6 quoted רב נחמן and replaces it with his real words.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The quote in step 6 claiming רב נחמן required half the length plus half the width.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It was wrongly attributed to רב נחמן; his real standard is ordinary livable space.

steps.title: How much space is 'as people normally live'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for an actual measurement behind רב נחמן's general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much is that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what "as people normally live" means in practice. This sets up the final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Normal living" is a general idea. The גמרא wants a concrete measure that a court could actually apply.

phrases.english: And how much?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the measurement behind step 7's rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical measure of normal living height.

steps.title: רב הונא: enough height to bring in a bundle of מחוזא reeds and turn around
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע sets the measure. The ceiling must be high enough to carry in a bundle of reeds, the kind used in מחוזא, and turn around with it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב יהושע said: So that the bundles of reeds of מחוזא can be brought in and turned around.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע answers step 8 with a practical measure for the lower floor's height.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the ceiling is too low to carry in a standard bundle of reeds and turn around with it, the space is no longer normally livable. At that point the agreement to rebuild applies.
steps.whatToRemember: The upstairs owner can block rebuilding, with two exceptions. The beams have sunk below ten טפחים, or the owners agreed to rebuild. Under an agreement, they rebuild once the lower floor is too low for normal living, meaning you can't carry in a bundle of מחוזא reeds and turn around.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two measurements. The answer of half the length plus half the width was rejected by רבה. The final standard is normal livable height.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּעָיְילִי אִיסּוּרְיָתָא דְמָחוֹזָא, וְהָדַר.
phrases.english: So that the bundles of reeds of Mechoza can be brought in, and one can turn around.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8's question.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Normal living height means enough room to bring in a bundle of מחוזא reeds and turn around.

steps.title: A wall built behind the neighbor's windows
steps.stepSummary: A man builds a wall right behind his neighbor's windows, and the neighbor complains that it darkens his house.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man was building a wall right behind his neighbor's windows. The neighbor said: You are making my house dark.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story and sets up the problem: a new wall is blocking a neighbor's light. This opens a long back-and-forth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The complaint is about losing light, not about land. The builder does not deny that he is blocking the light. Instead, he will try to fix it in a series of offers.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who was building a wall
behind his neighbor's windows.
The neighbor said to him: You are making my house dark.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה בָּנֵי אֲשִׁיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about building and a neighbor's rights, after the measurement given in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case: a new wall blocks a neighbor's windows, and the neighbor objects.

steps.title: First offer: new windows higher up
steps.stepSummary: The builder offers to seal the old windows and cut new ones above his wall. The neighbor says that would weaken his wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: The builder said: I will seal your windows here and make you new windows above my wall. The neighbor said: That will damage my wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The builder makes his first offer, and the neighbor turns it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The builder tries to keep the neighbor's light by moving the windows up. The neighbor answers that cutting new holes in his wall would weaken it.

phrases.english: He said to him: I will seal up your windows here,
and I will make you windows above my wall.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: קָא מַרַעְתְּ לֵיהּ לַאֲשִׁיתַאי.
phrases.english: He said to him: You will be damaging my wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָכַרְנָא לָךְ הָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The builder answers the complaint from step 10, and the neighbor rejects the answer.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Cutting new windows would weaken the neighbor's wall.

steps.title: Second offer: rebuild the top of the wall
steps.stepSummary: The builder offers to knock the neighbor's wall down to window level, rebuild it, and put windows higher up. The neighbor says a wall that is old below and new above won't last.
steps.simpleTranslation: The builder said: I will knock your wall down to where the windows are, rebuild it, and put windows in the new part above my wall. The neighbor said: A wall that is old at the bottom and new at the top won't stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The builder improves his offer, and the neighbor turns it down again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rebuilding the top answers the worry that holes would weaken the wall. The neighbor raises a new problem: mixing old and new sections makes the wall unstable.

phrases.english: He said to him: I will knock down your wall
down to where the windows are, and rebuild it,

phrases.aramaic: וְעָבֵידְנָא לָךְ כַּוֵּוי בְּבִנְיָנָא – לְעֵיל מֵאֲשִׁיתַאי.
phrases.english: and I will make you windows in the new part, above my wall.
He said to him: A wall that is old at the bottom
and new at the top will not stand.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָתַרְנָא לָךְ לַאֲשִׁיתָךְ עַד דּוּכְתָּא דְכַוֵּוי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An improved offer that answers the objection in step 11, followed by a new objection.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A wall that is half old and half new is unstable.

steps.title: Third offer: rebuild the whole wall
steps.stepSummary: The builder offers to rebuild the entire wall from the ground up. The neighbor says one new wall in an old house won't last.
steps.simpleTranslation: The builder said: I will knock the wall down to the ground, rebuild it, and make you windows in it. The neighbor said: One new wall in a house that is all old won't stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The builder goes further still, and the neighbor turns it down again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fully new wall fixes the problem of old and new parts in one wall. The neighbor now says the problem is one new wall standing in a house that is otherwise old.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: סָתַרְנָא לַהּ עַד לְאַרְעָא,
phrases.english: He said to him: I will knock it down to the ground,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָנֵינָא לַהּ, וְעָבֵידְנָא לָךְ כַּוֵּוי בְּגַוַּהּ.
phrases.english: rebuild it, and make you windows in it.
He said to him: One new wall
in a whole old house will not stand.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָתַרְנָא לַהּ עַד לְאַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in step 12, and is then rejected for a new reason.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: One new wall does not hold up well in an old house.

steps.title: Fourth offer: rebuild the whole house
steps.stepSummary: The builder offers to rebuild the neighbor's entire house with windows. The neighbor says he would have nowhere to live in the meantime.
steps.simpleTranslation: The builder said: I will knock down your whole house and build you windows in the new building. The neighbor said: I have no place to live.
steps.whatsHappening: The builder makes his biggest offer yet, and the neighbor turns it down because he would have nowhere to live.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A brand-new house fixes every building problem the neighbor raised. So the neighbor switches from a building problem to a living problem: he has nowhere to stay while it is built.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ: סָתַרְנָא לַהּ לְכוּלֵּיהּ בֵּיתָא,
phrases.english: He said to him: I will knock down the whole house,
and build you windows in the new building.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֵית לִי דּוּכְתָּא לְמֵידַר בַּהּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: I have no place to live in.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָתַרְנָא לַהּ לְכוּלֵּיהּ בֵּיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by rebuilding everything, and is rejected for a new reason.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The neighbor would be left without a home during the rebuilding.

steps.title: Last offer: renting him a place
steps.stepSummary: The builder offers to rent the neighbor a place to live. The neighbor simply says he does not want the bother.
steps.simpleTranslation: The builder said: I will rent you a place. The neighbor said: I don't want the trouble.
steps.whatsHappening: The builder answers the last complaint, and the neighbor refuses just because he does not want the hassle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every practical problem has now been solved. The neighbor's only remaining reason is that he does not want the trouble of moving, and this sets up רב חמא's ruling.

phrases.english: He said to him: I will rent a place for you.
He said to him: I don't want to go to the trouble.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָגַירְנָא לָךְ דּוּכְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 14, and the neighbor gives his final refusal.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The neighbor does not want to be troubled with moving.

steps.title: רב חמא: the neighbor may stop the wall
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא rules that the neighbor is legally entitled to stop the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חמא said: By law, he can stop him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חמא gives the ruling on the story: the neighbor wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even after all the generous offers, the neighbor does not have to accept any of them. Simply saying "I don't want the bother" is enough to stop the builder.
steps.whatToRemember: A person whose windows would be blocked can stop the new wall. He does not have to accept fixes that put him to trouble, even a rented place to live.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא: בְּדִין קָא מְעַכֵּב.
phrases.english: Rav Chama said: By law, he can stop him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָמָא: בְּדִין קָא מְעַכֵּב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the whole exchange in steps 10-15.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The neighbor may block the wall, even when he is offered a full rebuild and a rented place to live.

steps.title: Why do we need this story?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why this story is needed, since it seems the same as an earlier case.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the same as that case. Why do I need this one too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges whether this story teaches anything new, setting up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא sees this case as the same as an earlier one where a person could stop his neighbor's building. If the rule is already known, repeating it looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the same as that

phrases.aramaic: הַיְינוּ הָךְ – וְהָא תּוּ לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: This is the same as that case. Why do I need this one too?
phrases.notes: "That case" is the earlier case on the daf, where one owner could stop his neighbor from building.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיְינוּ הָךְ וְהָא תּוּ לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the ruling in step 16 needed to be taught.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for רב חמא's story.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It looks the same as an earlier case, so it seems to add nothing.

steps.title: Even a storage room counts
steps.stepSummary: The story teaches that the neighbor can object even if he only uses the room to store straw and wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us that even if he only uses the place for straw and firewood, he can still stop the wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by pointing out the new detail this story adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think losing light only matters in a room where people live. This story shows that even a storage room's light is protected.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us

steps.whatToRemember: The right to stop a wall that blocks the light applies even to a room used only for storage.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
that even though he uses it
only for straw and firewood.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New detail (hidden detail of the case)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think the right only applies to a room people live in.
steps.terutzMaskana: It applies even to a room used for storing straw and wood.

steps.title: Two brothers: a hall and a garden
steps.stepSummary: Two brothers divide an estate. The one who got the garden builds a wall in front of his brother's hall, and claims he is building on his own land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two brothers divided an estate. One got a hall and one got a garden. The one with the garden built a wall in front of the hall's opening. His brother said: You are darkening my house. He answered: I am building on my own property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story with a similar complaint, setting up another ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the two properties came from splitting one estate. The builder does not offer any fix; he only says he is building on his own land.

phrases.aramaic: הָנְהוּ בֵּי תְרֵי אַחֵי דְּפָלְגִי בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי;
phrases.english: There were two brothers who divided property with each other;

phrases.aramaic: חַד מַטְיֵיהּ אִסְפְּלִידָא, וְחַד מַטְיֵיהּ תַּרְבִּיצָא.
phrases.english: one got a hall, and one got a garden.
The one who got the garden went
and built a wall at the opening of the hall.
He said to him: You are making my house dark.
He said to him: I am building on my own land.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ בֵּי תְרֵי אַחֵי דְּפָלְגִי בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about a wall that blocks light, after the first story was settled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case: one brother builds on his share of the estate and blocks the other brother's light.

steps.title: רב חמא: the brother may build
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא rules that the brother with the garden is right and may build.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חמא said: He answered him correctly.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חמא rules on the second story, and this time the builder wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first story the neighbor could stop the wall. Here the builder's answer, "I am building on my own land," is accepted. The facts of this case differ: the two properties came from brothers dividing one estate. The next steps discuss why the builder may build.
steps.whatToRemember: Two rulings from רב חמא point in opposite directions. The neighbor could stop the wall in the first story, but the brother may build on his share of the estate in the second.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two rulings. In the first story רב חמא sides with the one whose light is blocked. In the brothers' story he sides with the builder.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא: בְּדִין קָאָמַר לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Rav Chama said: He answered him correctly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָמָא: בְּדִין קָאָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the story told in step 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The brother who received the garden may build the wall on his own share, even though it darkens his brother's hall.

steps.title: Why is this different from the vineyard and grain field case?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא challenges רב חמא's ruling using a ברייתא where a brother gets four אמות of working space in the other brother's field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: How is this different from the ברייתא? There, two brothers split an estate. One took a vineyard and one took a grain field. The vineyard owner gets four אמות in the grain field, because that was the understanding when they split. So why doesn't the hall owner keep his light here?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the ruling of step 20 by pointing to a ברייתא that seems to point the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, one brother's share comes with a built-in right to use part of the other brother's land. By that logic, the brother with the hall should also keep his right to light from the garden. So why can the garden brother block it?

keyTerms.meaning: An open field with no trees, usually planted with grain
Four אמות, the space needed to work the vineyard
They split the estate on that understanding

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
What is different from that which is taught (in a baraita):
Two brothers who divided (their father's estate),
one of them took a vineyard field
and one of them took a grain field:
the owner of the vineyard has
four cubits in the grain field,
because it was on that condition that they divided?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי, מַאי שְׁנָא מֵהָא דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב חמא's ruling in step 20 using a ברייתא
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חמא's ruling that the garden brother may block the hall's light
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the ברייתא, splitting an estate gives one brother rights in the other's land. So the hall brother should keep his light too.

steps.title: In the vineyard case, they priced it in
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that in the ברייתא the brothers priced their shares against each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to him: There, they compared the values of their shares and evened them out.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers רבינא. In the vineyard case, the brothers figured out what each share was worth, and the working space was part of that deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vineyard owner gets the four אמות because they were counted in the price when the shares were balanced. The answer suggests this did not happen in the hall-and-garden case.

keyTerms.meaning: They compared values with each other and evened out the shares

phrases.english: He (Rav Ashi) said to him:
There, they made an assessment with each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם דְּעַלּוּ לַהֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two cases are the same, so the hall brother should keep his light
steps.terutzMaskana: In the vineyard case the right was priced into the split

steps.title: Surely they priced the hall and garden too
steps.stepSummary: רבינא pushes back: no sensible brothers would split a hall and a garden without comparing their values.
steps.simpleTranslation: But here, what? Did they not compare values? Are we dealing with fools, where one took a valuable hall and the other took a cheap garden, and they never compared values?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks רב אשי's answer. Of course the brothers in the hall case also compared values.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A hall is worth much more than a garden, so the brothers must have balanced the shares. If they did, the hall's light should also count as part of the deal, and the difference רב אשי drew disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: A hall, a large open room

phrases.english: But here, what?
That they did not make an assessment with each other?
Are we dealing with fools,
that this one takes the hall
and that one takes the garden,
and they did not make an assessment with each other?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל הָכָא – מַאי, דְּלָא עַלּוּ לַהֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב אשי's answer in step 22
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that only the vineyard case was priced
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Sensible people would never split shares this unequal without balancing them, so the hall case was priced too.

steps.title: They priced the building, not the air
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that they priced the bricks, beams and boards, but not the airspace.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: True, they priced the bricks, beams and boards. But they did not price the airspace.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי sharpens his answer. The brothers did compare values, but only for the building itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deal covered the physical materials of the hall. The air and light coming in from the garden were never part of the price. So each brother keeps full control of his own airspace, and the garden brother may build.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב אשי, the brothers priced the building materials, not the air and light. So the hall owner has no built-in right to light from the garden. Step 25 raises a new challenge to this.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Granted that they made an assessment with each other
of the value of the bricks, beams and boards;
the value of the airspace they did not assess with each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: נְהִי דְּעַלּוּ לַהֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's pushback in step 23
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everything about the hall, including its light, was priced
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the materials were priced, not the airspace

steps.title: You gave me a hall and now it's a dark room
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the hall brother can't complain that his bright hall is being turned into a dark little room.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: At first you gave me a hall as my share, and now you are turning it into a small dark room!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge. The hall brother should be able to say he is being cheated out of what he received.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the air was never priced, the brother got something called a 'hall.' Blocking its light turns it into a different thing, a dark room. So it seems his share is being taken from him.

keyTerms.meaning: You gave me as my share

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
Originally you gave me a hall as my share,
now you are making it into a small dark room for me!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵימָא לֵיהּ: מֵעִיקָּרָא אִסְפְּלִידָא פְּלַגְתְּ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New challenge to the ruling after step 24's answer
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the garden brother may build
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The brother received a hall. Making it dark changes what he got.

steps.title: He only got the name 'hall'
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי answers that the brother only received something called a hall, not a promise that it stays bright.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי said: He only gave him the name.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר אשי answers the challenge. The brother received a room known as a 'hall,' and that is all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'hall' only identifies which room he got. It does not promise that the room will always stay a bright, open hall. So he has no claim when it gets darker.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said:
He just gave him the name as his share.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי: שְׁמָא בְּעָלְמָא פְּלַג לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 25
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Giving a 'hall' means promising a bright hall
steps.terutzMaskana: He only got a room that goes by the name 'hall'

steps.title: Sales that go by name only
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that a seller who uses a name like 'בית כור,' 'orchard' or 'vineyard' sells only the name, as long as the place is really called that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it taught: If someone says 'I am selling you a בית כור of soil,' the sale stands even if it is only half that size, because he only sold the name, as long as the place is called a 'בית כור.' 'I am selling you an orchard' stands even with no pomegranates, as long as it is called an orchard. 'I am selling you a vineyard' stands even with no vines, as long as it is called a vineyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רב שימי בר אשי's idea that someone can sell just a name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In each case, the name only points to which property is being sold. It does not promise that the property matches the name. This is meant to match the 'hall' that the brother received. The added condition is that the place must really be called by that name.

keyTerms.meaning: A field big enough to sow a kor of seed
It is his, and the sale stands
As long as it is called by that name

steps.whatToRemember: In a sale, a name only identifies the property. It does not promise its quality, as long as the place really goes by that name. The next step rejects using this for brothers who split an estate.

phrases.english: Isn't it taught (in a baraita):
One who says:
"I am selling you a beit kor of soil,"

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לֶתֶךְ – הִגִּיעוֹ,
phrases.english: even though it is only a letech, it is his,
phrases.notes: A לתך is half a כור, so the field is only half the size the name suggests.

phrases.english: because he sold him only the name;
and that is when it is called a "beit kor."
"I am selling you an orchard,"

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ רִמּוֹנִים – הִגִּיעוֹ,
phrases.english: even though there are no pomegranates in it, it is his,
because he sold him only the name;
and that is when it is called an "orchard."
"I am selling you a vineyard,"

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ גְּפָנִים – הִגִּיעוֹ,
phrases.english: even though there are no vines in it, it is his,
because he sold him only the name;
and that is when it is called a "vineyard"?!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי לָא תַּנְיָא, הָאוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב שימי בר אשי's answer in step 26
steps.raayaObject: The idea that a name used in a transfer only identifies the property
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא about selling a בית כור, an orchard and a vineyard
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a general rule about sales: a property's name identifies it but does not promise its quality.

steps.title: A sale is not like brothers splitting an inheritance
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from the seller who sells only a name. A buyer gets only the name, but a brother took his share expecting to live there the way their fathers did.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are these cases really the same?! There, the seller can tell the buyer: 'I only sold you the name.' Here, the brother who got the hall can say: 'I agreed to this split only because I expected to live in it the way our fathers lived there.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא from step 27. It says a sale and an inheritance split cannot be compared.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 26, רב שימי בר אשי said the brother got only something called a 'hall,' and step 27 brought support from a seller who sells only a name. Now the גמרא points out a key difference. A seller and buyer are strangers making a deal, so the buyer gets just what was named. Brothers splitting their father's house each expect things to stay as they were, so the hall brother expected his bright hall to stay bright.

keyTerms.meaning: Are they comparable? A standard way to reject a comparison
With this understanding, on this condition
I took my share (in the split)

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not attack the ברייתא itself. The ברייתא is still true for sales. The גמרא is only saying it cannot prove anything about brothers who split an inheritance.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that what each side expected matters. A split between heirs carries an unspoken understanding that a sale between strangers does not.

phrases.english: Are these comparable?!
There, he can say to him,
the seller to the buyer:
I sold you only the name;
phrases.notes: This is the seller case from the ברייתא in step 27, like 'vineyard' or 'orchard.'

phrases.english: here, he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the brother who got the hall, talking to the brother who got the garden.

phrases.english: I took my share on this understanding
that I would live in it
the way our fathers lived there.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the ברייתא proof brought in step 27 for רב שימי בר אשי's answer.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the ברייתא, and with it the support for רב שימי בר אשי's answer in step 26. The hall brother's claim from step 25 ('you gave me a hall') comes back. The ברייתא's rule about sales stays true.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A buyer gets only the name, but heirs split the estate expecting to keep living there as their fathers did. So the two cases are not alike.

steps.title: Setting up a new reply to רב חמא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new reply to רב חמא's ruling that the garden brother may build the wall. The content of the reply comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: This is only a setup line. The גמרא is opening a new reply to רב חמא, and the actual words come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the debate went back and forth about whether the hall brother can block the wall. Now someone turns directly to רב חמא with a response to his ruling. We have to wait for the next line to see exactly what they say.

phrases.english: They said to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is רב חמא, who ruled that the garden brother may build the wall. Their words continue in the next line.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof was rejected, the גמרא turns back to רב חמא's ruling with a new reply.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חמא's ruling that the garden brother may build a wall in front of the hall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only the opening formula appears here. The argument itself continues on the next amud.
